In mathematics, the '''Munn [[semigroup]]''' is the inverse semigroup of isomorphisms between principal ideals of a [[semilattice]] (a commutative semigroup of idempotents). Munn semigroups are named for the Scottish mathematician [[Walter Douglas Munn]] (1929–2008).<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Munn|title=Walter Douglas Munn}}</ref>

==Construction's steps==

Let <math>E</math> be a semilattice.

1) For all ''e'' in ''E'', we define ''Ee'':&nbsp;=&nbsp;{''i''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''E''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''e''} which is a [[principal ideal]] of&nbsp;''E''.

2) For all ''e'',&nbsp;''f'' in ''E'', we define ''T''<sub>''e'',''f''</sub> as the set of [[isomorphisms]] of ''Ee'' onto&nbsp;''Ef''.

3) The Munn semigroup of the [[semilattice]] ''E'' is defined as:  ''T''<sub>''E''</sub> :=&nbsp;<math>\bigcup_{e,f\in E}</math>&nbsp;{&nbsp;''T''<sub>''e'',''f''</sub> :&nbsp;(''e'',&nbsp;''f'')&nbsp;∈&nbsp;U&nbsp;}.

The semigroup's operation is composition of [[partial function|partial mappings]]. In fact, we can observe that ''T''<sub>''E''</sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''I''<sub>''E''</sub> where ''I''<sub>''E''</sub> is the [[symmetric inverse semigroup]] because all isomorphisms are partial one-one maps from subsets of ''E'' onto subsets of&nbsp;''E''.

The [[idempotent]]s of the Munn semigroup are the identity maps&nbsp;1<sub>''Ee''</sub>.

==Theorem==
For every semilattice <math>E</math>, the semilattice of idempotents of <math>T_E</math> is isomorphic to E.

==Example==
Let <math>E=\{0,1,2,...\}</math>. Then <math>E</math> is a semilattice under the usual ordering of the natural numbers (<math>0 < 1 < 2 < ...</math>).
The principal ideals of <math>E</math> are then <math>En=\{0,1,2,...,n\}</math> for all <math>n</math>. 
So, the principal ideals <math>Em</math> and <math>En</math> are isomorphic if and only if  <math>m=n</math>.

Thus <math>T_{n,n}</math> = {<math>1_{En}</math>} where <math>1_{En}</math> is the identity map from En to itself, and <math>T_{m,n}=\emptyset</math> if <math>m\not=n</math>. The semigroup product of <math>1_{Em}</math> and <math>1_{En}</math> is <math>1_{E\operatorname{min} \{m, n\}}</math>.
In this example, <math>T_E = \{1_{E0}, 1_{E1}, 1_{E2}, \ldots \} \cong E.</math>
